title: Apple Juice for a Hangover: Does It Help? (Why to Dilute It)
excerpt: Does apple juice help a hangover? What it can and can't do, why you should dilute it, how it compares to orange juice and Gatorade, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does apple juice help a hangover? Why diluting it matters, how it affects blood sugar and your stomach, and how it compares to other hangover drinks.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** apple juice can help a little with a hangover, mostly because it's an easy way to get fluid and some quick sugar into you when food sounds terrible. It isn't a cure, and there is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover. The best way to drink it is **diluted**, roughly half juice and half water. Full-strength apple juice is very sugary and naturally high in fructose and sorbitol, two sugars that can pull water into your gut and make an already unsettled stomach or loose stools worse. Watered down, it goes down easier, tastes good enough that you'll actually keep drinking, and still gives you a small lift in blood sugar.

**The quick rules:** Start with water. Once you're keeping fluids down, a glass of half-strength apple juice is a reasonable second drink. Sip it slowly rather than chugging it. Pair it with something bland like toast or crackers. If you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, an oral rehydration solution is the better tool, because apple juice has almost no sodium. And skip the "hair of the dog" versions like hard cider or an apple-flavored cocktail: more alcohol only pushes the hangover later.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangovers are miserable but harmless and fade within a day. Get medical help if you can't keep any fluids down for more than a few hours, you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you have black or bloody stools, you feel confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, you have a seizure, your heart is racing or beating irregularly and won't settle, you have severe or worsening stomach pain, or you have signs of serious dehydration like very little urine, dizziness when you stand, or a dry mouth that won't go away. If someone is unconscious, breathing slowly or irregularly, or can't be woken, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. If you have diabetes and take insulin or a sulfonylurea, watch for low blood sugar the morning after drinking and treat it promptly. And if you regularly feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious the morning after drinking and only feel better once you drink again, tell a doctor. That pattern is worth a conversation and is very treatable.

## Does Apple Juice Help a Hangover?

A hangover isn't one problem. It's a bundle of them that hit at once: mild dehydration, an irritated stomach, poor sleep, an inflammatory response, a drop in blood sugar for some people, and the leftover effects of acetaldehyde, the toxic compound your body makes while breaking down alcohol. No single drink touches all of that.

Apple juice helps with a couple of pieces:

- **Fluid.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more than you drink. Any drink you'll actually finish helps replace some of that. Apple juice is mild, familiar, and easy to sip, which matters when plain water feels like a chore.
- **Quick carbohydrates.** An 8-ounce glass of unsweetened apple juice has roughly 25 grams of sugar. If your blood sugar dipped overnight, that can take the edge off shakiness, weakness, and that hollow, light-headed feeling.
- **A bit of potassium.** Apple juice has a modest amount of potassium, less than orange juice or coconut water, but more than water.

What apple juice doesn't do:

- It doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol in any meaningful way.
- It doesn't "detox" your liver. Your liver handles that on its own schedule.
- It doesn't replace sodium, which is the main electrolyte you lose through sweat, vomiting, and diarrhea.
- It doesn't fix the headache, the poor sleep, or the inflammation.

So think of apple juice as a comfort drink with a few useful properties, not as a treatment. If it's what you feel like drinking, it's a fine choice. Just drink it the smart way.

## Why You Should Dilute Apple Juice

This is the single most useful thing to know about apple juice and hangovers. Full-strength apple juice has three features that can work against you the morning after.

**1. It's concentrated sugar.** A tall glass of apple juice can carry as much sugar as a can of soda. When you drink a lot of sugar quickly, your body can respond with a sharp rise in blood sugar followed by a dip, which some people feel as a second wave of tiredness. Diluting it spreads that sugar out.

**2. It's high in fructose.** Apples are naturally rich in fructose, and apple juice has noticeably more fructose than glucose. Your small intestine absorbs fructose more slowly than glucose, and absorbs it best when glucose is present alongside it. When there's extra fructose, some of it reaches your large intestine unabsorbed, pulls water in, and gets fermented by gut bacteria. The result can be gas, bloating, cramping, and loose stools. Plenty of people have a limited capacity to absorb fructose even on a good day.

**3. It contains sorbitol.** Apples also contain sorbitol, a sugar alcohol that's poorly absorbed. Sorbitol is the reason prunes, pears, and apple juice have a reputation for loosening the bowels. It's also why pediatricians have long cautioned that too much apple juice can cause diarrhea in toddlers.

Now add alcohol to the picture. Alcohol already speeds up how fast things move through your gut and irritates the intestinal lining, which is why so many people get [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking). Pouring a big glass of undiluted apple juice on top of that can make it worse.

Diluting cuts all three problems roughly in half while keeping the taste and some of the sugar. There's also decent research support for the idea in a different setting. A randomized trial published in *JAMA* in 2016 (Freedman and colleagues) compared half-strength apple juice with a commercial electrolyte solution in children with mild gastroenteritis and minimal dehydration. The children given diluted apple juice, followed by whatever fluids they preferred, did at least as well, likely because they were happier to keep drinking it. That trial was about stomach bugs in kids, not hangovers in adults, so it doesn't prove anything about hangovers. But it supports the basic point: when you're mildly dehydrated, a diluted drink you'll actually finish can beat a "better" drink you won't.

## How to Make Diluted Apple Juice for a Hangover

Keep it simple.

**Basic half-strength apple juice**

- 1 cup (240 ml) apple juice
- 1 cup (240 ml) water
- Ice, if you like it cold

Mix and sip over 20 to 30 minutes. Cold drinks are often easier to tolerate when you feel queasy.

**Apple juice with a pinch of salt**

If you've been sweating a lot or had a bout of loose stools, you can add a small pinch of table salt (about 1/8 teaspoon) to the half-and-half mix. The salt adds sodium, which helps your body hold on to fluid, and the small amount of sugar helps the gut absorb that sodium. It won't taste like a sports drink, but it shouldn't taste salty either. If it tastes noticeably salty, you've added too much. This is a rough home version, not a medical oral rehydration solution. If you're losing a lot of fluid, a properly formulated product is better. Our guide to a [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) walks through more careful ratios.

**Sparkling apple spritzer**

Mix apple juice with plain sparkling water instead of still water. Some people find the bubbles settling. Others find carbonation adds to bloating. If your stomach is very full or gassy, stick with still water.

**Apple juice ice chips or popsicles**

If you've been vomiting, freeze diluted apple juice into ice cubes or popsicle molds the night before (or in an hour if you're patient). Sucking on ice chips delivers fluid slowly, which is easier on a stomach that rejects big gulps.

### How much to drink

There's no magic number. A reasonable approach is to alternate: a glass of water, then a glass of diluted apple juice, then water again. Small, steady sips beat large amounts at once. Your urine is a useful guide. Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Dark yellow means keep going. If you're barely urinating at all after several hours of trying to drink, that's a sign to get help.

## Apple Juice and Low Blood Sugar After Drinking

One part of the hangover where juice genuinely makes sense is blood sugar.

When your liver is busy breaking down alcohol, it's less able to make new glucose, a process called gluconeogenesis. Normally your liver releases glucose overnight to keep your blood sugar steady while you sleep. After a night of drinking, especially if you didn't eat much, that system can lag, and blood sugar can drift lower than usual by morning. Most healthy people don't drop into a dangerous range, but a modest dip can add to weakness, shakiness, irritability, and fatigue.

A small glass of juice is a quick way to bring that up. Because it's a liquid, it absorbs fast, which is also why juice is a standard choice for treating mild low blood sugar in people with diabetes.

A few cautions:

- **Don't overdo it.** A huge amount of juice on an empty stomach can cause a fast spike and a fall afterward. Have a moderate glass, then follow with real food that has some protein and starch, like eggs and toast. Our article on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why they're a solid choice.
- **If you have diabetes,** alcohol makes blood sugar harder to predict for many hours, and juice can push it up quickly. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, check your levels the morning after drinking and treat lows the way your care team has taught you. Our [guide to alcohol and blood sugar with diabetes](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers this in detail.
- **Low blood sugar that doesn't respond** to juice and food, or that comes with confusion or trouble staying awake, needs medical attention.

## Apple Juice and an Upset Stomach

Here apple juice has a real advantage over some other juices, with one big catch.

**The advantage:** apple juice is less acidic than orange juice or grapefruit juice. It still has some acid, mostly malic acid, but many people find it gentler on a stomach that's burning from drinking. If you have [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking), diluted apple juice is often easier to tolerate than orange juice. Our piece on [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) explains why citrus can sting.

**The catch:** the fructose and sorbitol problem. If your hangover shows up as cramping, gas, or diarrhea, undiluted apple juice is one of the worse choices you can make. In that case, water, an oral rehydration solution, or plain broth is a better first drink, and you can try heavily diluted apple juice later once things settle.

**If you're nauseous,** sip rather than drink. Wait 10 to 15 minutes after vomiting before trying any fluid. Start with a few spoonfuls or ice chips. If those stay down, slowly increase. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ways to calm your stomach, and [ginger](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) is worth a try alongside it.

## Apple Juice vs. Other Hangover Drinks

Here's how apple juice stacks up against the drinks people most often reach for. These are rough comparisons. Exact amounts vary by brand and serving size, so check the label on what you actually have.

| Drink | Sodium | Sugar | Acidity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Water | None | None | Neutral | Baseline rehydration; always a good start |
| Apple juice (diluted) | Very low | Moderate | Mildly acidic | Easy fluid plus a little quick sugar |
| Apple juice (full strength) | Very low | High | Mildly acidic | Not ideal; may upset the gut |
| Orange juice | Very low | High | More acidic | Vitamin C and potassium; may sting with heartburn |
| Coconut water | Low to moderate | Low to moderate | Mild | Potassium; light flavor |
| Sports drinks | Moderate | Moderate to high | Mildly acidic | Fluid after sweating; some sodium |
| Oral rehydration solutions | Higher | Low | Mild | Vomiting, diarrhea, or real dehydration |

**Apple juice vs. orange juice.** Orange juice has more vitamin C and more potassium. Apple juice is usually gentler on heartburn but harder on loose stools because of the fructose and sorbitol. If your main problem is a burning stomach, apple juice may be kinder. If your main problem is diarrhea, neither juice is a great first choice.

**Apple juice vs. Gatorade.** Sports drinks have sodium, which apple juice lacks, and sodium is what helps your body hold on to the fluid you drink. If you sweated a lot or had diarrhea, a sports drink edges out apple juice. If you just want something pleasant to sip, apple juice is fine. See our [Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover) breakdown for more.

**Apple juice vs. coconut water.** Coconut water has more potassium and less sugar, and it's less likely to upset your gut. It also has more sodium than apple juice, though still less than a proper electrolyte drink. More in our [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide.

**Apple juice vs. Pedialyte or other oral rehydration solutions.** These are built specifically for dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea, with a balance of sodium and sugar designed for absorption. If you're actively losing fluid, they're the better choice. Apple juice is more of a "feeling a bit rough and want something tasty" drink.

**Apple juice vs. plain water.** For most mild hangovers, water does the heavy lifting. Apple juice is a supplement to water, not a replacement. Our piece on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) explains what water can and can't do.

## Clear vs. Cloudy Apple Juice

Supermarkets sell two main kinds of apple juice:

- **Clear apple juice** has been filtered to remove pulp and particles. It's the classic golden juice in most cartons.
- **Cloudy apple juice** (sometimes sold as unfiltered or "apple cider" in the US) keeps more of the apple solids.

Cloudy juice generally keeps more of the apple's plant compounds, called polyphenols, which are antioxidants. That sounds appealing for a hangover, since inflammation and oxidative stress are part of the picture. But there's no good evidence that the polyphenols in a glass of apple juice make any noticeable difference to how hungover you feel. The amounts are modest, and a lot of the research on apple polyphenols comes from lab studies or long-term diet studies, not hangovers.

Pick whichever you prefer. The sugar content is similar, and both are better diluted.

### Should you pick "no sugar added"?

Yes, when you can. "100% juice" or "no sugar added" means the sugar comes from the apples themselves. "Apple juice drink," "apple juice cocktail," or "apple-flavored beverage" often means added sugar and sometimes very little real juice. Those are worse for your blood sugar and your gut.

### What about vitamin C?

Apples aren't naturally a rich source of vitamin C, and much of it is lost in processing. Many brands add vitamin C back, partly to keep the juice from browning, so the label is the only way to know. Either way, there's no good evidence that extra vitamin C fixes a hangover. Our [vitamins for a hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) guide covers what the research actually shows.

## Apple Cider, Hard Cider, and Apple Cider Vinegar

The word "cider" causes a lot of confusion, so here's the short guide.

**Sweet apple cider** (the non-alcoholic kind sold in the fall in the US) is essentially unfiltered apple juice. Treat it the same way: fine in moderation, better diluted.

**Hard cider** is alcoholic, usually somewhere around beer strength. Drinking it the morning after is a form of "hair of the dog." A bit of alcohol can briefly dull hangover symptoms because your body is in mild withdrawal from last night's drinking, but it only postpones the hangover and adds more alcohol for your liver to process. It's a bad habit to build. The same goes for apple-based cocktails, brunch ciders, and apple brandy.

**Apple cider vinegar** is a popular internet hangover hack, usually as a shot in water. There is no good evidence that apple cider vinegar helps with hangovers. It's quite acidic, so it can irritate a stomach and esophagus that are already raw from drinking, and undiluted vinegar can damage tooth enamel. If you want to try it, dilute it heavily and don't take it on an empty, queasy stomach. Honestly, plain diluted apple juice is a better bet. Our roundup of [viral hangover cures](/never-hungover/viral-hangover-cures-tested-science-2025) looks at more of these trends.

## Is a Whole Apple Better Than Apple Juice?

For most purposes, yes, if you can face it.

A whole apple gives you the same natural sugars but with fiber, which slows down how fast the sugar hits your bloodstream and makes it easier on your gut. It's also more filling. The downside is obvious: when you're nauseous, chewing a crunchy apple can feel impossible, and the fiber may not be welcome if you already have loose stools.

A good compromise is **applesauce**. It's soft, mild, easy to swallow, and a classic part of bland diets used for upset stomachs. Unsweetened applesauce with a slice of plain toast is a gentle breakfast when you're not up for much else. For more ideas, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) and our look at [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover), which pair well with applesauce.

## Who Should Be Careful With Apple Juice

Apple juice is safe for most people, but a few groups should think twice.

- **People with diabetes or prediabetes.** Juice raises blood sugar quickly, and alcohol makes blood sugar unpredictable for hours afterward. Use juice to treat a confirmed low, not as a casual hangover drink, and talk to your doctor about how to handle drinking.
- **People with IBS or fructose malabsorption.** Apple juice is high in fructose and sorbitol, which are common triggers. Many people following a low-FODMAP diet are advised to limit apples and apple juice. Choose a different drink.
- **People with frequent heartburn or reflux.** Apple juice is gentler than citrus, but it's still acidic. Dilute it and have it with food.
- **People watching their calories or weight.** The calories in juice add up quickly on top of the calories from the night before. Water first, juice as a small extra.
- **Anyone taking medication.** Apple juice is not known for the strong drug interactions that grapefruit juice causes. That said, some fruit juices, including apple and orange, can reduce the absorption of a few medicines, such as the allergy drug fexofenadine (Allegra), which is labeled to be taken with water. If you take prescription medication regularly, check the label or ask a pharmacist. And never use juice to wash down pain relievers on top of alcohol without thinking about which pain reliever you're taking.

## A Simple Morning-After Plan With Apple Juice

If you wake up hungover and apple juice sounds good, here's a sensible order:

1. **Drink a glass of water** as soon as you're up. If you're queasy, take small sips.
2. **Have a glass of half-strength apple juice** once water stays down. Sip it over 20 to 30 minutes.
3. **Eat something bland** within the next hour: toast, crackers, applesauce, a banana, or eggs if you can manage them.
4. **Keep alternating** water and diluted juice through the morning. Add a pinch of salt to the juice, or switch to an electrolyte drink, if you've been sweating, vomiting, or have loose stools.
5. **Rest.** Sleep after drinking is usually poor quality, so a nap or an early night does more than any drink.
6. **Skip more alcohol.** No hard cider, no mimosas, no hair of the dog.

If you're not improving by the afternoon, or any of the warning signs in the box at the top show up, get medical advice.

For more help, our [complete guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide) covers the whole recovery process, and our list of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares more options side by side.

## The Bigger Picture: Preventing the Next One

Apple juice can make a hangover a little more comfortable. It can't undo the night before. The things with the strongest support for a better morning happen before and during drinking: eating a real meal first, pacing yourself, alternating each alcoholic drink with water, and simply drinking less. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best support, and our piece on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why food matters so much.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven, and it doesn't replace eating, hydrating, or drinking less. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main products.

For how apple juice stacks up against every other option, see our [best juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-juice-for-hangover) ranking, and our guide to [cranberry juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/cranberry-juice-for-hangover) for a lower-sugar comparison.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is apple juice good for a hangover?**

It can help a little. It gets fluid and some quick sugar into you when you don't feel like eating, and it's milder on the stomach than citrus juice. It isn't a cure, and there is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover. Drink it diluted with about the same amount of water, and drink plain water too.

**Why should I dilute apple juice when I'm hungover?**

Full-strength apple juice is high in sugar, especially fructose, and contains sorbitol. Both can pull water into your gut and cause gas, cramps, or loose stools, which alcohol already makes more likely. Mixing it half and half with water keeps the taste and some of the sugar while making it much easier on your stomach.

**Does apple juice help with diarrhea after drinking?**

Undiluted, it can make diarrhea worse because of its fructose and sorbitol. If you have loose stools after drinking, start with water, an oral rehydration solution, or broth. Heavily diluted apple juice is usually fine once things settle. If diarrhea is severe, bloody, black, or lasts more than a couple of days, see a doctor.

**Is apple juice or orange juice better for a hangover?**

It depends on your symptoms. Apple juice is less acidic, so it's often easier on heartburn. Orange juice has more vitamin C and potassium but can sting a burning stomach. Apple juice is more likely to upset loose bowels. Neither has much sodium, so if you've been vomiting or sweating a lot, an electrolyte drink is a better choice than either.

**Does apple juice help with low blood sugar after drinking?**

Yes, a small glass is a quick way to raise mildly low blood sugar, which can contribute to shakiness and weakness the morning after. Follow it with real food so your blood sugar doesn't dip again. If you have diabetes, check your levels and follow your care team's plan. Confusion or trouble staying awake needs medical attention.

**Does apple cider vinegar cure a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that apple cider vinegar helps a hangover. It's very acidic, so it can irritate a stomach already upset by alcohol, and undiluted vinegar can harm tooth enamel. Diluted apple juice with water is a gentler and more pleasant choice.

**Is hard cider a good hangover cure?**

No. Hard cider contains alcohol, so drinking it the morning after is a form of hair of the dog. It may briefly dull symptoms, but it only delays the hangover and gives your liver more alcohol to process. Stick with non-alcoholic drinks.

**Is applesauce good for a hangover?**

Unsweetened applesauce is a good choice if you're queasy. It's soft, mild, and easy to swallow, and it provides some carbohydrates with a little fiber. It pairs well with plain toast or a banana as a gentle first meal.
